newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German corruption wave prompts tough action.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German corruption wave prompts tough action.

text.p: A stream of corporate corruption scandals in Germany has dented its self-image as a by-the-rules player and spurred a fresh drive to clamp down on malpractice.

The government plans to introduce tighter penalties for corruption -- doubling the maximum prison term for convicted civil servants to 10 years -- and is considering blacklisting errant companies from public service contracts.

Public prosecutors are pushing to be allowed to use more powerful methods to crack major corruption rings, such as tapping telephone lines and offering informants the incentive of a reduced or waived sentence.

Corruption has become a hot topic in Germany in recent years but public consternation reached new heights last summer when prosecutors revealed a probe into more than 200 people at 40 companies, among them 65 past and present staff at General Motors Corp subsidiary Opel.

A second big scandal emerged this year as work ended on Frankfurt Airport's second terminal. Prosecutors mounted a massive investigation into a suspected corruption network of up to 50 managers, inluding airport staff and 20 contractors.
Experts say corruption has always played a quiet role in German business, but the stakes have risen dramatically, especially in the battle for major public service contracts.

While a fur coat or expensive dinner might have bought success in a public tender in the 1970s, prosecutors say some government officials are now demanding cash payments of thousands or even millions of marks just for information.

Reliable figures are hard to find, but prosecutors estimate the annual cost of corruption in the public building sector alone at five to 10 billion marks -- a figure which gives the cash-strapped government an added incentive for a clampdown.
In the state of Hesse, which includes the business capital of Frankfurt, systematic bribery costs the state finances between 120 million marks ($79.45 million) and 170 million marks a year.

"Compared with France or Italy, for example, the situation is fairly limited. But that doesn't change the fact that the level of corruption here -- for our society and with our legal system -- is dramatic and emotionally unacceptable," said Frankfurt senior public prosecutor Wolfgang Schaupensteiner.

Schaupensteiner heads a nine-year-old specialist corruption task force -- Germany's first ever -- and says he is deluged with work. His division has probed 1,700 corruption cases to date and brought around 340 to court.

"We have over 300 cases pending," he said in an interview. "Every time one of our investigators clears up one case, it leads to dozens more, like an avalanche. That shows just how widespread corruption is.
"In most cases this is not just the site foreman getting a backhander. There are top level people, right up to management board level, dealing very personally with bribery," he said.

The Frankfurt airport case alone, where losses on overpriced contracts and payments for non-existent deliveries are estimated at tens of millions of marks, is so much broader than it seemed at first that investigations will drag on at least until 1998, Schaupensteiner said.

The scandals, continually highlighted in the media, have exploded Germany's belief that its public servants and business executives were above the kind of wheeling and dealing more associated with their more chaotic Mediterranean neighbours.

"Controls must be sharpened if the state is not to suffer lasting damage ... But the roots are in society's moral code ... If it is viewed as chic to bribe here and cheat a bit there, a corruption-free society remains a dream," the Berliner Morgenpost newspaper said in a recent editorial.

Industry groups have issued their members with guidelines on how to break chains of bribery in their organisations and improve controls, but observers say a hard core of executives views corruption as part and parcel of everyday life.

"Ask anyone who deals with the German building sector, for example, about an anti-corruption drive and you will just get a tired smile and a shrug of the shoulders," said Karen Hussmann, editor of Berlin-based Transparency International, a quarterly newsletter on corruption worldwide.

The building industry, where cash-strapped companies struggle furiously to win lucrative public contracts, has been at the heart of most big German corruption cases. A major probe into a contruction scam in Frankfurt in the late 1980s emptied offices and sites throughout the city for months.

Engineering group Siemens suffered serious embarrassment last year when it was among five companies banned from doing business in Singapore for five years after being accused of involvement in the country's biggest ever corruption ring.
Prosecutors claim to have discovered hundreds of smaller scale scams involving residence permits, driving licences, market stall licences and public sector housing.

Even the medical profession is not immune. Prosecutors said this July they were investigating 1,860 doctors and health executives on suspicion of accepting 33 million marks in bribes to buy overpriced replacement heart valves and other equipment.
The German cabinet in June approved a draft corruption law making price-fixing deals between firms tendering for contracts a criminal offence punishable with up to five years' prison.

The proposals, which should be finalised this year, also raise the penalty for bribery in business to five years from one year and impose a maximum 10 years for giving or accepting bribes or gratuities in the public service sector.
Prosecutors have welcomed what they say is overdue action from Bonn but say the government should take a tougher line.

Schaupensteiner is pushing for a broader definition of corruption to include the "soft-soaping" to which he says government officials are continually exposed -- a suggestion Bonn has so far rejected as impracticable.

Prosecutors and other justice officials have also called for reduced sentences for individuals who inform on a corruption ring, an almost unheard of occurrence at present because of the danger of prosecution.

"Principles like free competition are also at stake here, not just state funds. We have to stop corporate crime and corruption from gaining a stronger foothold here," said Schaupensteiner. ($1=1.5103 Mark)
